case.request: When a reserved item becomes available for pickup, patrons who have opted in to SMS should get a text message in addition to the existing hold-ready email. We already have the Twilio account and the opt-in flag on patron profiles (sms_opt_in). The text should include the title, the pickup branch, and the pickup-by date, which is 7 days after the item becomes available. Don't send texts between 9pm and 8am branch local time; queue them and send at 8am. If the SMS send fails, rely on the email alone and log the failure. The only UI change is a small 'SMS sent' indicator in the staff hold-detail view.
case.rationale: Channel, consent flag, content, quiet hours, failure handling and UI scope are all specified, so an engineer can start immediately.

answers.Q1: Use the patron profile's existing mobile phone field (mobile_phone), normalised to E.164. If an opted-in patron has no valid or SMS-capable number, skip the SMS, send the email as usual, and log the skip with reason 'no_valid_mobile'; do not flag it to staff.
answers.Q2: Every text must identify the library by name and end with 'Reply STOP to opt out'. Use Twilio's built-in opt-out handling, and also process its inbound STOP/START webhook to set sms_opt_in to false/true on the patron profile with a timestamp. Never send to a number Twilio reports as opted out.

requirements: When a reserved item becomes available for pickup, a patron who has opted in to SMS receives a text message.
SMS opt-in is determined by the existing sms_opt_in flag on the patron profile.
SMS messages are sent through the existing Twilio account.
The existing hold-ready email continues to be sent; the SMS is in addition to it.
Patrons who have not opted in to SMS (sms_opt_in not set) receive no hold-ready text and get only the existing email.
The text message includes the item title, the pickup branch, and the pickup-by date.
The pickup-by date is 7 days after the item becomes available.
No hold-ready texts are sent between 9pm and 8am branch local time.
Texts that would otherwise go out during the 9pm-8am quiet window are queued and sent at 8am branch local time.
If the SMS send fails, the system relies on the hold-ready email alone (no alternative channel) and logs the failure.
The staff hold-detail view shows a small 'SMS sent' indicator.
No UI changes are made other than the 'SMS sent' indicator in the staff hold-detail view.
The hold-ready SMS is sent to the number in the patron profile's existing mobile phone field (mobile_phone), normalised to E.164.
If an opted-in patron has no valid or SMS-capable number, the SMS is skipped, the email is sent as usual, and the skip is logged with reason 'no_valid_mobile'; the skip is not flagged to staff.
Every hold-ready text identifies the library by name and ends with 'Reply STOP to opt out'.
Twilio's built-in opt-out handling is used.
The system processes Twilio's inbound STOP/START webhook to set sms_opt_in to false (STOP) or true (START) on the patron profile, recording a timestamp of the change.
The system never sends a hold-ready SMS to a number that Twilio reports as opted out.

case.request: Growers want to set a low soil-moisture threshold per field in the mobile app: a percentage between 5 and 60, default 20. Sensors report every 15 minutes. When any sensor in a field reports below that field's threshold for two consecutive readings, send a push notification to every user assigned to that farm. Don't alert again for the same field within 6 hours unless moisture has recovered above the threshold in between. Any change to a threshold should be written to the field's activity log with who changed it and the old and new values.
case.rationale: Range, default, trigger rule, recipients, debounce and audit are explicit; remaining details are implementer choices.

answers.Q1: The two consecutive below-threshold readings must come from the same sensor. Consecutive means that sensor's next reading by sensor timestamp; if the gap between them exceeds 30 minutes (one missed reading), the pair does not count. Discard out-of-order readings older than the sensor's latest processed reading for alerting purposes.
answers.Q2: Moisture has recovered when every sensor that was below threshold in the field reports a reading above the threshold; one such reading per sensor is enough. A reading exactly equal to the threshold counts as not below, so it neither triggers an alert nor counts as recovered.
answers.Q3: Only users with the farm owner or farm manager role may change a field's threshold. Any other attempt is rejected with a permission error, makes no change, and is recorded in the field's activity log as a denied attempt.

requirements: The mobile app shall let growers set a low soil-moisture threshold for each field individually.
The threshold shall be a percentage between 5 and 60, and shall default to 20 when no value has been set.
An alert condition shall be raised for a field when any sensor in that field reports a moisture value below the field's threshold for two consecutive readings.
When the alert condition is raised, a push notification shall be sent to every user assigned to the farm that contains the field.
After an alert for a field, no further alert shall be sent for the same field within 6 hours, unless moisture has recovered above the threshold in between.
Every change to a field's threshold shall be written to that field's activity log, recording who made the change and the old and new values.
Alert evaluation shall work with sensor readings reported at a 15-minute cadence. The source sets no latency or processing-model requirement.

The two consecutive below-threshold readings that raise an alert shall come from the same sensor. Consecutive means that sensor's next reading by sensor timestamp; if the gap between the two readings exceeds 30 minutes, the pair shall not count.
For alerting purposes, out-of-order readings older than the sensor's latest processed reading shall be discarded.
Moisture shall be considered recovered for a field when every sensor that was below threshold in the field reports a reading above the threshold; one such reading per sensor is sufficient.
A reading exactly equal to the threshold shall count as not below; it shall neither contribute to triggering an alert nor count as recovered.
Only users with the farm owner or farm manager role shall be permitted to change a field's threshold.

Any threshold change attempt by a user without the farm owner or farm manager role shall be rejected with a permission error, shall make no change, and shall be recorded in the field's activity log as a denied attempt.

work_items.title: Inventory existing settings, push, farm-assignment and activity-log components
work_items.description: Scope: research only, with no code changes. No repository or evidence was supplied (Q8). Determine whether these already exist: a mobile field-settings screen, a push notification channel with device registration, farm user assignments with owner/manager roles, and a per-field activity log. Expected output: a written findings note. For each component it records exists/absent, its location if found, and the integration impact on W3, W4 and W7. Approach: inspect the target codebase(s) once a repository is identified. Record unknowns rather than assuming components exist. Q7 operational cases (delivery failures, retries, users with no device, farms with no users) are listed as design inputs for W7 and are not decided here.
criteria: A findings note states, for each of the four components (field settings screen, push channel, farm user assignments with roles, per-field activity log), whether it exists. For each existing component it cites a concrete location. For each absent component it states it is absent.

work_items.title: Per-field threshold data model with 5–60 range and default 20
work_items.description: Scope: persist one low soil-moisture threshold percentage per field and validate it on the server. Expected behavior: a field with no stored value resolves to an effective threshold of 20. Values outside the 5–60 range are rejected with a validation error and nothing is stored. Approach: add a nullable per-field threshold, or an equivalent, with a resolver that returns 20 when unset. Validation lives in a shared server-side function used by W2. Bound inclusivity and decimal precision are open (Q4, non-blocking). The implementer must document the chosen rule, and tests must follow that documented rule. How the default is stored feeds Q6 (old value logged on first set).
criteria: For a field with no stored threshold, the effective threshold resolves to 20.
Values clearly inside the range (e.g. 6, 20, 59) are accepted and stored. Values outside it (e.g. 4, 61, -1) are rejected with a validation error and leave the stored value unchanged.
The handling of the exact boundaries 5 and 60 and of decimal values is documented as an implementer default pending Q4, and is covered by tests that match the documented rule.

work_items.title: Field activity log entries for threshold changes and denied attempts
work_items.description: Scope: write entries to the field's activity log. Expected behavior: every successful threshold change writes one entry with the acting user, the old value and the new value. A denied attempt writes an entry marked as denied, with the acting user. Approach: provide a log-writer function called from the W2 update path in the same unit of work as the change, so a successful change always has an entry. The integration target depends on the W0 findings about whether a per-field activity log exists. The old value recorded on the first change from the default (20 vs 'unset') is open (Q6, non-blocking). The implementer must document the chosen representation.
criteria: After a successful threshold change from value A to value B on a field, exactly one new entry exists in that field's activity log. The entry contains the acting user's identity, old value A and new value B.
The old-value representation for the first change from the default is documented as an implementer default pending Q6, and is covered by a test matching that rule.

work_items.title: Authorized threshold update endpoint (owner/manager only)
work_items.description: Scope: a server-side operation to change a field's threshold. Expected behavior: users with the farm owner or farm manager role for the field's farm may change the threshold, subject to W1 validation, and the change is logged via W3. Any other user receives a permission error. In that case the threshold is not changed and a denied-attempt entry is written to the field's activity log. Approach: check the role server-side before validation and persistence. The role is resolved from the farm user assignments identified in W0. Enforcement must not rely on the mobile UI.
criteria: A user with the farm owner role and a user with the farm manager role can each change a field's threshold to a valid value, and the new value is persisted.

A user assigned to the farm without the owner or manager role, and a user not assigned to the farm, each receive a permission error when changing the threshold. In both cases the stored threshold is unchanged.
Each rejected attempt writes one entry to the field's activity log marked as a denied attempt, identifying the acting user.
Calling the update operation directly, bypassing the mobile UI, as a non-owner/manager is rejected identically.

work_items.title: Mobile app per-field threshold setting screen
work_items.description: Scope: a mobile UI that shows and edits the threshold for each field individually. Expected behavior: the screen shows the field's effective threshold, which is 20 when unset. Owners and managers can submit a new value via the W2 operation. Validation and permission errors returned by the server are displayed, and no change is shown as saved. Approach: extend or create a field settings screen according to the W0 findings. Client-side checks are convenience only; the server stays authoritative.
criteria: In the mobile app, setting a threshold on field A changes only field A's displayed and stored threshold. Field B on the same farm keeps its own value.
When the server returns a permission error or a validation error, the app displays the error and continues to show the previously stored value.

work_items.title: Alert trigger evaluation on per-sensor consecutive readings
work_items.description: Scope: evaluate incoming sensor readings and raise a field alert condition. Expected behavior: a field alert condition is raised when one sensor reports two consecutive readings strictly below the field's effective threshold. Consecutive means that sensor's next reading by sensor timestamp, and the gap must not exceed 30 minutes. Readings from different sensors never form a pair. A reading equal to the threshold is not below and breaks the pair. Out-of-order readings older than that sensor's latest processed reading are discarded for alerting. Approach: keep per-sensor state (last processed timestamp and whether it was below), updated on each reading. The design must work with the 15-minute reporting cadence; no latency target is set (Q9, open). Offline-sensor handling is open (Q7, non-blocking) and is documented as a default.
criteria: With threshold 20, a sensor reporting 18 then 17 fifteen minutes apart raises an alert condition for its field after the second reading. A single reading of 18 does not.
Sensor X reporting 18 followed by sensor Y in the same field reporting 17 does not raise an alert condition.
Two below-threshold readings from the same sensor 30 minutes apart raise the condition. Readings 45 minutes apart do not.
A reading whose sensor timestamp is older than that sensor's latest processed reading is discarded: it neither forms nor breaks a pair, and it does not update the sensor's state.
With threshold 20, a sensor reporting 18, then exactly 20, then 18 does not raise an alert condition. A reading equal to the threshold is not below.

work_items.title: 6-hour per-field alert suppression with recovery reset
work_items.description: Scope: decide whether a raised alert condition results in an alert. Expected behavior: after an alert for a field, further alert conditions for that field within 6 hours are suppressed, unless moisture has recovered in between. Moisture has recovered when every sensor that was below threshold in the field has reported at least one reading strictly above the threshold. A reading equal to the threshold does not count as recovery. Once recovered, a new alert condition may alert even within 6 hours. Approach: keep per-field state holding the last alert time and the set of sensors still below threshold. Two items are open and non-blocking, so the implementer must document a chosen default for each: inclusivity at exactly 6 hours (Q5), and the effect of a threshold change during an active window (Q6).
criteria: After an alert at time T for a field, a new alert condition at T+3h with no intervening recovery produces no alert. A new alert condition at T+6h15m produces an alert.

In a field where sensors X and Y were both below threshold, X recovering above the threshold while Y has not does not lift suppression. Once Y also reports a reading above the threshold, a new alert condition at T+2h produces an alert.
A single above-threshold reading per previously-below sensor is enough for recovery. A reading exactly equal to the threshold does not count as recovery.
The behavior at exactly T+6h (Q5) and on a threshold change during a suppression window (Q6) is documented as an implementer default, with tests matching the documented rules.

work_items.title: Push notification fan-out to all users assigned to the farm
work_items.description: Scope: deliver an alert that W6 permits as a push notification. Expected behavior: every user assigned to the farm containing the field receives a push notification identifying the field. Approach: resolve the farm's assigned users and send via the push channel identified in W0. Several Q7 cases are open and non-blocking: the time at which recipients are resolved, delivery failures and retries, users with no registered device, and farms with no users. Each is documented as a reviewed default and is not decided here.
criteria: For a permitted alert on a field of a farm with three assigned users, a push notification identifying the field is sent to all three users. Users not assigned to that farm receive none.
The handling of delivery failure/retry, users without a device, farms with no users, and recipient-resolution time is documented as defaults pending Q7.

review_findings: No work item defines or tests whether a sensor that stays below threshold keeps raising new alert conditions on later readings (a third, fourth, ... consecutive below reading). S5/R5 imply a re-alert once the 6-hour window expires if the field is still dry. W6-AC1 assumes a 'new alert condition at T+6h15m', but W5 neither specifies nor tests how such a condition arises without recovery. Add a W5 criterion covering continued below-threshold readings after the initial pair, and a W6 test showing that a continuously dry field re-alerts after 6 hours.

Under R10, recovery requires every sensor 'that was below threshold' to report above the threshold. The reference point is undefined. It could mean below at the time of the alert, below at any point since the alert, or currently below. W6 keeps a 'set of sensors still below threshold' but does not say how a sensor that drops below after the alert affects the set. This can be resolved as a documented implementer default or a follow-up question. No acceptance criterion pins it down.

W2's description says roles are resolved from the farm user assignments identified in W0, but W2 does not list W0 as a direct dependency. It is satisfied only transitively through W3. Declare W0 explicitly for clarity. Similarly, W1's persistence approach depends on W0 findings about the existing data model, but W1 has no dependency on W0.

No repository or repository evidence was supplied. Every work item has repository_id null, and W0 cannot produce its required concrete locations until a repository is identified. W3, W4 and W7 are gated on W0. Integration claims about the push channel, role model and activity log are therefore ungrounded (Q8). Tier 3 risk is appropriately retained.

Denied-attempt log entries appear in two places. W3's description scopes them in, but W3's requirement_ids (R6 only) and its criteria do not cover them, while W2-AC3 (R13) does. Responsibility for the denied-attempt log format is split across the two items and is ambiguous. Either add R13 to W3 with a criterion, or remove denied-attempt logging from W3's scope.

R7's text contains a non-requirement statement: 'The source sets no latency or processing-model requirement.' This was carried over from the base. It belongs in an assumption or in Q9, not in the requirement text. This is minor and does not change behaviour.

case.request: We need to make the permit process faster for small businesses. Council has been getting complaints about signage and patio permits taking eight weeks. Can we add some kind of fast track? Maybe some permits get auto-approved and reviewed afterwards, or maybe applicants pay an extra fee for priority review, I'm not sure which. The planning department says they're open to ideas, but whatever we do has to hold up if a neighbour challenges a decision. Ideally something is live before spring.
case.rationale: Whether the mechanism is post-hoc auto-approval or a paid priority lane, and which permits qualify, changes what is built, involves money and carries legal exposure.

answers.Q1: Build a free 'express review' track: eligible applications go to a dedicated review queue with a 10-business-day decision target, decided by a planner before approval. Do not build auto-approval with after-the-fact review, and do not build a priority fee.
answers.Q2: Eligibility is limited to signage and patio permits. A small business is one with fewer than 50 employees holding a current city business licence; the applicant self-declares on the form and staff verify the licence number against the city business licence register during review.
answers.Q3: Every express decision is made by a qualified planner before approval, keeps the existing neighbour notification and comment period required by the bylaws, records written reasons, preserves the existing appeal window, and retains the full decision file under the current permit retention schedule. City legal must confirm the shortened timeline complies with the bylaws before launch.
answers.Q4: No priority fee will be charged. The express track uses the standard permit fee, so no new payment handling or refund policy is needed.

requirements: Provide a fast-track process that reduces processing time for small business permit applications, covering at least signage and patio permits, which currently take eight weeks.
Decisions made through the fast-track process must be legally defensible if a neighbour challenges them.
Record the basis, decision-maker or rule, timestamp and any subsequent review for each fast-track decision, so a challenged decision can be reconstructed and defended.
Target having the fast-track capability live before spring.
Build a free 'express review' track: eligible applications go to a dedicated review queue with a 10-business-day decision target, decided by a planner before approval.
Do not build auto-approval with after-the-fact review, and do not build a priority fee.
Express track eligibility is limited to signage and patio permits.
A small business is one with fewer than 50 employees holding a current city business licence; the applicant self-declares this on the application form.
During review, staff verify the applicant's business licence number against the city business licence register.
Every express decision is made by a qualified planner before approval and keeps the existing neighbour notification and comment period required by the bylaws.
Each express decision records written reasons, preserves the existing appeal window, and retains the full decision file under the current permit retention schedule.
City legal must confirm the shortened timeline complies with the bylaws before launch.
No priority fee will be charged; the express track uses the standard permit fee, so no new payment handling or refund policy is needed.

work_items.title: Express track eligibility and application intake for signage and patio permits
work_items.description: Scope: add an express review option to the permit application intake for small businesses. Behaviour: the express option is offered only for signage and patio permit applications (R7). The applicant self-declares on the form that the business has fewer than 50 employees and holds a current city business licence, and enters the licence number (R8). Express applications are charged the standard permit fee, with no priority fee and no new payment or refund handling (R13, R6 fee part). This intake is the entry point of the fast-track process that shortens processing time for small business permits (R1). Approach: extend the existing application form and validation to capture the express flag, self-declaration and licence number. Reuse the existing fee calculation unchanged. No repository, file paths or tests were supplied, so the implementer must locate the intake and fee code. Out of scope: queue routing and licence verification (W2), and decision records (W3).
criteria: The express review option can be selected only when the permit type is signage or patio. It is not offered, and is rejected server-side, for any other permit type.

An express application cannot be submitted unless the applicant completes a self-declaration of fewer than 50 employees and a current city business licence, and supplies a licence number. All three are stored with the application.
The fee charged for an express application equals the standard permit fee for the same permit type. No priority fee, surcharge, new payment path or refund rule is introduced.

work_items.title: Dedicated express review queue with planner decision and licence verification
work_items.description: Scope: route express applications into a dedicated review queue worked by planners. Behaviour: express applications enter a separate queue that tracks a 10-business-day decision target (R5). No approval is issued until a qualified planner records a decision; there is no auto-approval and no after-the-fact review path (R6, R10 planner part). During review, staff verify the self-declared licence number against the city business licence register and record the verification result (R9). The existing neighbour notification and comment period required by the bylaws still runs for express applications, and approval cannot be issued before it closes (R10). Approach: add a queue or status for express applications, add business-day due-date computation, gate the approval action on a qualified planner role, a recorded licence verification and a closed comment period, and reuse the existing notification workflow. No repository evidence was supplied. Whether the register check is manual lookup or system integration is an implementation choice to confirm with planning staff.
criteria: Every submitted express application appears in the dedicated express queue, separate from the standard queue. Its decision due date is computed as 10 business days from the start point defined for the queue.
An express application can only reach approved status through an explicit decision by a user holding the qualified planner role. No automatic approval or approve-then-review path exists.
Approval of an express application is blocked until staff record the result of verifying the licence number against the city business licence register.
Express applications trigger the same neighbour notification as standard applications. Approval is blocked until the bylaw-required comment period has elapsed.

work_items.title: Defensible express decision record, appeal window and retention
work_items.description: Scope: make each express decision reconstructable and defensible if a neighbour challenges it. Behaviour: each decision stores the deciding planner, the decision timestamp, the written reasons (mandatory), the licence verification result, the notification and comment-period dates, and any later review or appeal events (R3, R11). The existing appeal window applies unchanged to express decisions (R11). The full decision file is retained under the current permit retention schedule (R11). Together these support the legal defensibility of decisions (R2). Approach: extend the decision data model and planner UI with a required reasons field. Apply the existing appeal-window logic and retention policy to express records rather than creating new rules. Provide an export or view of the complete decision file. No repository evidence was supplied.
criteria: An express decision cannot be saved without written reasons. Each saved decision records the deciding planner, the timestamp, the reasons, the licence verification result, and the notification and comment-period dates.
Any subsequent review or appeal of an express decision is appended to the decision file with its actor and timestamp. The original decision is not overwritten.
Express decisions receive the same appeal window as standard decisions for the same permit type. Express decision files are subject to the current permit retention schedule.
For a sample express decision, a complete decision file can be produced that lets a reviewer reconstruct who decided, when, on what basis, and what notification occurred.

work_items.title: Express processing-time reporting against the eight-week baseline
work_items.description: Scope: measure whether the express track actually shortens processing time. Behaviour: report, for express signage and patio applications, the elapsed time from submission to decision and the share decided within the 10-business-day target. Compare this with the current eight-week baseline for standard applications (R1, R5). Approach: derive the metrics from the queue and decision timestamps produced by W2 and W3, and expose them in a report or dashboard. Q5 (the overall fast-track processing-time target) remains a non-blocking open question. The report uses the 10-business-day decision target from the Q1 answer and should show the configured target so it can be adjusted once Q5 is confirmed. No repository evidence was supplied.
criteria: A report shows, per permit type (signage and patio), the median and per-application elapsed time from submission to decision for express applications, alongside the standard-track figures.
The report shows the percentage of express applications decided within 10 business days. Applications that miss the target are listed.

work_items.title: City legal bylaw confirmation and pre-spring launch readiness
work_items.description: Scope: launch gate for the express track. Behaviour: before launch, obtain written confirmation from city legal that the shortened express timeline complies with the bylaws (R12). This supports defensibility against neighbour challenges (R2). Track launch readiness against the goal of going live before spring (R4). Q6 (the exact go-live date and whether it is a hard deadline) is non-blocking and open, so the plan records the date as unconfirmed rather than inventing one. Approach: assemble a legal review package (express workflow, timeline, notification and appeal handling, decision record sample from W3). Record the legal confirmation. Enable the express option for applicants only after confirmation is recorded. This ticket does not obtain or fabricate the legal approval; it tracks it.
criteria: Written confirmation from city legal that the shortened express timeline complies with the bylaws is recorded before the express option is enabled for applicants.
The express option stays disabled for applicants until the legal confirmation is recorded.
A launch plan exists that targets go-live before spring, lists the remaining work and the date of legal review, and explicitly marks the exact go-live date as pending answer to Q6.

review_findings: The 10-business-day decision target (R5) may conflict with the existing bylaw-required neighbour notification and comment period (R10). W2-AC4 blocks approval until that period closes. If the period is close to or longer than 10 business days, the target cannot be met. The plan does not state the comment-period length or reconcile the two. This depends on the pending city legal confirmation (R12, W5), which has not been obtained.

W2-AC1 computes the due date as 10 business days 'from the start point defined for the queue', but no start point is defined. It could be submission, completeness check or queue entry. The criterion is not testable as written, and W4 reporting depends on the same definition. The business-day calendar, including holidays, is also unspecified.

No behaviour or criterion covers an express application whose licence verification fails or whose self-declaration is false. Options include rejecting it, moving it to the standard queue, or refusing it. W2-AC3 only requires that a result is recorded before approval.

Q5 (the target processing time) is kept open and A2 calls it unresolved, yet the authenticated Q1 answer already sets a 10-business-day decision target. It is unclear whether Q5 is meant to cover something different, such as end-to-end time including the comment period. W4 treats the target as adjustable, but the relationship between the two should be clarified.

R3 (preserved safe_inference) still refers to 'decision-maker or rule' and 'subsequent review'. Both stem from the auto-approval option that R6 now rejects. W3 interprets these as planner identity and appeal or review events, which is reasonable, but the stale wording could invite rule-based decisions. This is acceptable because original requirements must be preserved.

W5 (legal confirmation and launch gate) depends on W4 (processing-time reporting). Reporting is not needed for the legal review package, and this edge may needlessly delay the legal confirmation on the critical path to a pre-spring launch (R4).

W2-AC3 and W2-AC4 are marked directly_stated, but gating approval on a recorded verification goes beyond the answer. The Q2 answer only says staff verify during review. The approval gating is an inference and would more accurately be labelled safe_inference.

The 'qualified planner role' is used as an authorization gate (W2-AC2, R10), but which staff qualify, and how the role is assigned, is not defined. It is also unclear whether the 'staff' who verify licences (R9) must be planners.

There is no repository context. All work items have a null repository_id and implementers must locate the intake, fee, queue, notification and retention components. Risk correctly remains tier 3, and the launch depends on a city legal confirmation that has not been obtained.

case.request: Clinicians keep asking for a way to loop other people into a video visit. Sometimes that's a family member, sometimes an interpreter, sometimes a provider from a different clinic who isn't on our platform. Can we build this? It should be simple, maybe a link the clinician sends. I don't know whether the guest should be able to see the chart or the visit notes, or whether we need the patient's consent each time someone joins. Let's get something on the board for next sprint.
case.rationale: Guest access to health records and patient consent are undecided and determine who can see personal health data and the legal obligations involved.

answers.Q1: No. Guests of any type (family member, interpreter, external provider) get video and audio only, with no access to the chart, visit notes or any other record in the platform. External providers who need records get them through the existing records-release process.
answers.Q2: Yes. The clinician must obtain the patient's verbal consent before admitting each guest, every time someone joins, and confirm it in a required checkbox that records guest name, guest type, clinician, and timestamp in the visit record. Interpreters from our contracted interpreter service also require this consent.
answers.Q3: Each guest link is single-use, tied to one visit, and expires at the end of the visit or 24 hours after creation, whichever comes first. Guests enter their name and wait in a waiting room until the clinician admits them, and the clinician can remove a guest at any time. Visits are capped at 3 guests.

requirements: Clinicians can invite additional participants (guests) into an existing video visit.
Supported guest types include family members, interpreters, and providers from a different clinic.
Guests who do not have an account on the platform (e.g., external providers) must be able to join the video visit.
The invite flow should be simple for clinicians, potentially a link the clinician sends to the guest.
Guest access to the patient's chart and visit notes must follow an approved rule; the guest data-access scope is undecided.
Patient consent requirements for guests joining a visit must be defined and enforced per the approved rule (including whether consent is required each time someone joins).
Guests of any type (family member, interpreter, external provider) get video and audio only, with no access to the chart, visit notes or any other record in the platform.
External providers who need records get them through the existing records-release process, not through the guest video visit.
The clinician must obtain the patient's verbal consent before admitting each guest, every time someone joins.
The clinician must confirm patient consent in a required checkbox before a guest is admitted; confirmation records guest name, guest type, clinician, and timestamp in the visit record.
Interpreters from the contracted interpreter service also require patient consent before being admitted.
Each guest link is single-use and tied to one visit.
Each guest link expires at the end of the visit or 24 hours after creation, whichever comes first.
Guests enter their name and wait in a waiting room until the clinician admits them.
The clinician can remove a guest from the visit at any time.
Visits are capped at 3 guests.
review_findings: W5 depends only on W2. W5-AC1 requires that the guest UI show video and audio only for the visit, and W5-AC2 covers external providers inside an active guest session. case.request: Bug: the roster validator accepts pairings that break the 10-hour minimum rest rule when the rest period spans a DST change. The validator computes 10h20 of rest; the real elapsed time is 9h20 because clocks went forward at 01:00. It looks like we subtract local wall-clock times. Expected: compute rest in UTC and flag the pairing as illegal. Please add regression tests for both spring-forward and fall-back, and produce a one-off report of currently published rosters in the next 30 days that are affected.
case.rationale: Reproduction, root cause, expected behaviour, tests and a follow-up report are all stated.

answers.Q1: Resolve naive local times using the crew base's IANA time zone. For an ambiguous time, choose the offset that gives the shortest computed rest; for a nonexistent time, reject the pairing as invalid and flag it for manual review. The validator must never resolve a time in a way that makes rest look longer.
answers.Q2: Include only crew ID, pairing ID, duty end and report times in UTC and local time, computed rest, and shortfall; no names or contact details. Deliver it only to the crew scheduling manager and the compliance officer via the restricted crew-ops shared drive, not email, and delete it after 90 days.

Add regression tests covering rest periods that span both a spring-forward and a fall-back DST transition.
Produce a one-off report of currently published rosters in the next 30 days that are affected by the DST rest-calculation bug.

Naive local duty end and report times must be resolved to UTC using the crew base's IANA time zone.

work_items.title: Compute minimum-rest period as real UTC elapsed time in the roster validator
work_items.description:
Scope: change the roster validator's rest calculation, the interval between duty end and the next report, so it uses real elapsed time between UTC instants. This replaces any wall-clock subtraction. The validator must flag a pairing as illegal when that UTC rest is below the 10-hour minimum.

Approach:
- Locate the validator's rest computation and confirm how duty end and report timestamps are stored. This is open question Q3: UTC, offset-aware, or naive local. S6 ('subtract local wall-clock times') is an unverified diagnosis.
- Convert both endpoints to UTC instants, then subtract.
- Where timestamps are naive local values, resolve them with the crew base's IANA time zone (R7, from the Q1 answer).
- The implementer must record in the PR whether stored naive times are base-local or station-local. If they are station-local, applying the crew base zone (R7) could give wrong instants for away-from-base duties. That conflict must be raised to the approver rather than silently resolved (review finding F2).
- Do not change the existing 10h boundary comparison operator (Q7 is open; keep current behaviour).

Out of scope:
- Ambiguous and nonexistent local times: W2.
- The broader regression suite: W3.

No repository was supplied. File paths, entry points and test commands are unknown and must be identified by the implementer.
criteria: For C-4471, duty end 2026-03-29 00:30 Europe/Lisbon and next report 10:50 Europe/Lisbon the same day, the validator computes rest of exactly 9h20 (00:30Z to 09:50Z) and flags the pairing as illegal.

The rest duration the validator compares against the 10-hour minimum equals the difference between the UTC instants of duty end and next report. This holds for every timestamp storage form found in the code (UTC, offset-aware, or naive local).
Naive local duty end and report times are converted to UTC using the crew base's IANA time zone.
The 10-hour boundary comparison (e.g. treatment of exactly 10h00) is unchanged from the pre-fix code.

work_items.title: Conservative resolution of ambiguous and nonexistent local times
work_items.description:
Scope: extend the UTC conversion from W1 for naive local times that are ambiguous (repeated during a fall-back) or nonexistent (in a spring-forward gap) in the crew base's IANA zone.

Expected behaviour (from the Q1 answer):
- Ambiguous time: choose whichever offset gives the shortest computed rest for the pairing. Never resolve a time in a way that makes rest look longer.
- Nonexistent time: reject the pairing as invalid and flag it for manual review.

Approach:
- Evaluate both candidate offsets for an ambiguous endpoint and keep the minimum rest.
- Detect gap times and emit an invalid / manual-review outcome through the validator's existing result mechanism, which the implementer must identify.

Units tests for these two cases live in this ticket, not in W3 (review finding F6).

Open point (finding F8): who receives and acts on the manual-review flag is not specified. Do not invent a recipient; surface it in the PR for the approver.
criteria: When duty end is an ambiguous local time (e.g. 01:30 Europe/Lisbon on 2026-10-25), the validator uses the offset that yields the shorter rest. A test where the two offsets would give different rests asserts the shorter value is used for the legality check.
When duty end or report is a nonexistent local time (e.g. 01:30 Europe/Lisbon on 2026-03-29), the validator returns an invalid result flagged for manual review and does not return a legal result.

work_items.title: Spring-forward and fall-back DST regression tests for rest calculation
work_items.description:
Scope: add regression tests to the validator test suite for rest periods spanning a spring-forward transition and a fall-back transition. Unambiguous endpoint times are used; ambiguous and gap cases are covered in W2.

Test cases (Europe/Lisbon, IANA rules):
- Spring-forward: the C-4471 case. Duty end 2026-03-29 00:30, report 10:50. Expect 9h20 rest, illegal.
- Fall-back: duty end 2026-10-25 00:30, report 09:00. Expect 9h30 rest (23:30Z to 09:00Z), illegal.

Tests assert the corrected outcome only. They do not assert the pre-fix behaviour, because S6's wall-clock diagnosis is unverified (Q3, finding F1).

A fall-back case where correct UTC computation makes a previously rejected pairing legal is a permissive change; Q4 is open. It must not be added as a blocking assertion. If added, mark it in the PR for reviewer confirmation (finding F3).
criteria: The spring-forward regression test (C-4471, Europe/Lisbon 2026-03-29 00:30 to 10:50) asserts computed rest 9h20 and an illegal result, and passes after W1.
The fall-back regression test (Europe/Lisbon 2026-10-25 00:30 to 09:00) asserts computed rest 9h30 and an illegal result, and passes after W1.
No regression test in W3 asserts a pairing becoming legal because of the fall-back correction while Q4 remains unanswered.

review_findings: W3-AC3 keeps permissive-case assertions out of the regression tests. However, the blocking W1-AC2 criterion still requires the production validator to use UTC instant differences. case.request: Since the 14 September release, about 2,300 residential customers on the time-of-use tariff were billed twice for the August cycle. The invoice batch job retried after a database timeout and didn't check whether invoices had already been issued. Roughly 900 of those customers pay by autopay and their cards have already been charged twice. We obviously need to make the retry idempotent, but we also have to decide what happens for affected customers: refund to card, account credit, or let them choose, and whether and how we notify them. Finance and the regulatory team haven't weighed in yet.
case.rationale: The remediation moves customer money and has regulatory implications that the request explicitly leaves undecided.

answers.Q1: Autopay customers charged twice get an automatic refund of the duplicate charge to the original card within 5 business days; no choice flow. For all ~2,300 affected customers, void the duplicate invoice so each account shows only one August invoice; the ~1,400 non-autopay customers need no money movement, and any who already paid twice are refunded to the original payment method.
answers.Q2: Yes. Email every affected customer within 5 business days (letter by post where no email is on file) stating the duplicate was an error, the duplicate invoice is void, and, for autopay customers, the refund amount and date. The regulatory team will file the incident with the energy regulator per its billing-error reporting rules before notices go out.

requirements: The invoice batch job's retry behaviour must be idempotent: retrying after a failure such as a database timeout must not issue duplicate invoices.
Before issuing an invoice, including on retry, the invoice batch job must check whether an invoice has already been issued for that customer and billing cycle, and must skip issuance if one exists.
Identify the affected customers: the residential time-of-use customers who were invoiced twice for the August cycle. Also identify the subset of autopay customers whose cards were charged twice.

Provide remediation for affected customers, including the autopay customers charged twice. The method has not been decided; the options are refund to card, account credit, or letting the customer choose.
Decide whether and how affected customers are notified of the duplicate billing and its remediation, and implement the approved approach.
Autopay customers whose cards were charged twice must automatically receive a refund of the duplicate charge to the original card within 5 business days. No customer choice flow is provided.
For all ~2,300 affected customers, void the duplicate August invoice so each account shows only one August invoice.
The ~1,400 non-autopay affected customers need no money movement, except that any who already paid twice must be refunded the duplicate payment to their original payment method.
Notify every affected customer by email within 5 business days. Where no email is on file, send a letter by post instead.
The notice must state that the duplicate was an error and that the duplicate invoice is void. For autopay customers, it must also state the refund amount and date.
Customer notices must not be sent until the regulatory team has filed the incident with the energy regulator under its billing-error reporting rules.

work_items.title: Make invoice batch job retry idempotent with a pre-issuance existing-invoice check
work_items.description: Scope: the invoice batch job whose retry after a database timeout re-issued August-cycle invoices without checking whether invoices had already been issued (S2). Expected behavior: before issuing any invoice, including on retry, the job checks whether an invoice already exists for that customer and billing cycle and skips issuance if one exists (R2). Retrying after any failure, such as a database timeout, must never produce a second invoice for the same customer and cycle (R1). Approach: add an idempotency guard on invoice issuance, enforced both in the job's existence check and, where the data store supports it, by a uniqueness constraint so concurrent or partial retries cannot slip through. The exact idempotency key and whether the fix extends beyond time-of-use residential customers are open in non-blocking Q3. The engineer should choose and document a reasonable default, at minimum customer account plus billing cycle. No repository evidence was supplied, so no file paths or existing tests are cited.
criteria: An automated test simulates a database timeout after invoices have been written for a batch, then triggers the job's retry. After the retry, exactly one invoice exists per customer per billing cycle, and none of those invoices was issued twice.

For a customer and billing cycle that already has an issued invoice, the issuance path, both on first run and on retry, skips issuance and records the skip. An automated test also covers the case where no prior invoice exists, in which case one invoice is issued.

The chosen idempotency key, and the decided scope of tariffs and segments covered by the guard, are documented in the change description. They are labelled as an engineering default pending non-blocking Q3.

work_items.title: Produce reconciled list of affected August-cycle customers and autopay double-charge subset
work_items.description:
Scope: identify the roughly 2,300 residential time-of-use customers invoiced twice for the August cycle (S1). - original and duplicate invoice IDs
- autopay flag
- duplicate charge or payment amount and payment reference
- original payment method
- email-on-file flag
- postal address availability

work_items.title: Void duplicate August invoices for all affected customers
work_items.description: Scope: per Finance's answer to Q1, void the duplicate August invoice for every affected customer in the W2 list, so that each account shows exactly one August invoice (R7). criteria: After the run, every account in the W2 affected list shows exactly one non-void August invoice, and the duplicate invoice is in a void state.
Re-running the void process makes no additional changes, and no original (non-duplicate) invoice is voided.

work_items.title: Automatically refund duplicate autopay card charges to original card within 5 business days
work_items.description: Scope: for each autopay customer in W2 whose card was charged twice, issue one automatic refund of the duplicate charge amount to the original card, within 5 business days (R6). This is part of R4. There is no customer choice flow and no account-credit alternative, per Finance's answer to Q1. Approach: a batch refund run against the W2 autopay subset, keyed on the duplicate charge reference so each charge can be refunded at most once. It should support a dry run and a Finance-reviewed preview, because card refunds are effectively irreversible. Refund amount and date are recorded per account for the notice content in W7. All refunds are issued within 5 business days, measured from the window start date confirmed by Finance.
The refund process issues refunds without any customer action, and re-running it cannot refund the same duplicate charge twice.
The refund amount and refund date are stored per autopay account for use in the notification.

work_items.title: Refund non-autopay customers who already paid the duplicate invoice twice
work_items.description: Scope: the roughly 1,400 non-autopay affected customers need no money movement, apart from voiding the duplicate invoice, which W3 handles (R8). The exception is any non-autopay customer flagged in W2 as having already paid twice. Each of those customers is refunded the duplicate payment to their original payment method. This is part of R4. Approach: a batch refund run limited to the W2 non-autopay double-payer set. It is keyed on the duplicate payment reference to prevent repeat refunds, with a dry run and Finance-reviewed preview. No credits or adjustments are applied to other non-autopay accounts.
criteria: Each non-autopay account that paid twice receives exactly one refund of the duplicate payment amount to its original payment method.
No refund, credit or other money movement is applied to non-autopay affected accounts that did not pay twice.

work_items.title: Gate customer notices on the regulatory team's filing with the energy regulator
work_items.description: Scope: per the regulatory team's answer to Q2, the regulatory team files the incident with the energy regulator under its billing-error reporting rules before any customer notice goes out (R11). Together with W7, this completes the decided notification approach (R5). Engineering scope: provide the incident facts the filing needs, drawn from W2 counts and the W1 root-cause summary. Implement and record a hard gate that blocks the W7 send until the regulatory team records confirmation that the filing was made. Engineering neither performs nor approves the filing itself.

The record shows the regulatory filing timestamp is earlier than the first customer notice timestamp.

work_items.title: Notify all affected customers by email, or by post where no email is on file, within 5 business days
work_items.description:
Scope: per the answer to Q2, notify every affected customer in W2 within 5 business days (R9). Notices go by email, or by postal letter where no email is on file. This implements the approved notification approach (R5). Required content (R10):
- the duplicate was an error
- the duplicate invoice is void
- for autopay customers, the refund amount and date from W4

Approach: generate notices from the W2 list, using W3 void status and W4 refund data. Route each notice by email-on-file and track delivery per account. The send only runs after the W6 regulatory gate is satisfied. The answer does not state the date from which the 5 business days are counted. That date, and its interaction with the filing-first gate, must be confirmed with the regulatory team before sending, without assuming a value.
criteria: Every affected account receives exactly one notice: by email where an email is on file, otherwise by postal letter. All notices are sent within 5 business days of the confirmed window start date.
Every notice states that the duplicate was an error and that the duplicate invoice is void. Every autopay notice also states that customer's refund amount and refund date, matching the W4 records.
No notice is sent before the W6 filing confirmation is recorded.

review_findings: The start date for the 5-business-day windows is not recorded in any authenticated answer. This applies to the refund window in R6 and the notice window in R9. The R9 notice deadline may conflict with R11's filing-first rule. Under R11 the regulatory team must file before any notice is sent, and that filing is outside engineering control. If the filing is late, the 5-business-day notice obligation in R9 could become impossible to meet. No escalation path or owner is defined for this case.

No criterion checks that the combination of voiding and refunding leaves each account correctly balanced. For autopay customers and non-autopay double payers, voiding a paid duplicate invoice (W3) may create an account credit or negative balance in the billing system. A separate refund (W4/W5) would then remediate the customer twice. W3 asserts that voiding moves no money, but no acceptance criterion checks post-remediation balances: no residual credit and no outstanding duplicate amount.

The W2-AC2 criterion goes beyond its cited requirement. It requires flagging non-autopay customers who already paid twice, which comes from the Q1 clarification (R8), not from R3. Yet the criterion cites only R3 and is marked directly_stated. It should also cite R8, or W2 should include R8.

W7-AC3 enforces the filing-before-notice ordering from R11 but cites only R5, and W7's requirement_ids omit R11. It is also classed as verification_kind security_check, although it is an ordering or compliance check.
W6 is missing a dependency on W1. W6's description says the filing facts draw on the W1 root-cause summary, but W6 depends only on W2.

Card refund failure cases are not addressed. W4 has no defined handling for an original card that is expired, closed or rejects the refund. The Q1 answer forbids a choice flow and an account-credit alternative, so a fallback for failures needs a Finance decision rather than an engineering default.

The preserved texts of R4 and R5 still say the method and notification approach are undecided, and the objective says decisions are pending. These are now resolved by R6–R11.
